nodes.label: A lock protects an invariant, not a statement
nodes.rationale: Locking only the write is pointless because the stale value was already read. The critical section must span every step that assumes the balance has not changed — ask 'what am I assuming stays true?' and lock that whole span.

nodes.label: Lock granularity: global vs per-account vs per-field
nodes.rationale: Granularity is the dial between correctness and throughput. One global lock is correct but serialises the whole bank; per-field is fastest but makes deadlock very likely. Per-entity (per account, via ConcurrentDictionary<Guid, SemaphoreSlim>) is the sweet spot: only same-account requests queue.

nodes.label: SemaphoreSlim rather than lock
nodes.rationale: You cannot await inside a lock block: a monitor is owned by the thread that entered it, and an await may resume on a different thread that would release a lock it never took. SemaphoreSlim(1,1) is owned by nobody so any continuation can release it. The cost is no reentrancy and no ownership — every acquire needs exactly one release, guarded here by Interlocked.Exchange because a double release raises the count and silently admits two actors.

nodes.label: Never hold a lock across I/O you don't control
nodes.rationale: Pessimistic coordination converts other people's latency into your own. If the critical section calls an external provider taking 2 seconds, every other request for that account waits 2 seconds. Do the slow call outside the lock and re-validate inside it.

nodes.label: In-process lock: correct on one instance, silently broken on three
nodes.rationale: The semaphore dictionary is a field on one object in one process. Three replicas hold three separate semaphores for the same account id, so there is no mutual exclusion at all — the lost update returns with code that looks correct. This is the hinge of the whole repo; the strategy reports scalesAcrossInstances:false. The fix is not a better lock but moving coordination to shared state (database or distributed lock) behind the same IAccountLock interface.
